title: Why is Roman concrete still standing after 2,000 years?

post.caption: Ancient Rome, episode 8: the Pantheon dome, self-healing Roman concrete, the Via Appia, the Pont du Gard and an aqueduct that still feeds the Trevi Fountain. Images: public domain / CC0 (Panini, Piranesi, Hubert Robert, Rijksmuseum), AI illustrations marked. Map data: Natural Earth.

beats.speaker: a
beats.text: Our concrete cracks in decades. This Roman dome has stood 1,900 years.
beats.say: Our concrete cracks in decades. This Roman dome has stood nineteen hundred years.

beats.speaker: q
beats.text: Why is Roman concrete still standing after 2,000 years?
beats.say: Why is Roman concrete still standing after two thousand years?

beats.speaker: a
beats.text: Mostly thanks to volcanic ash, and a trick scientists only figured out recently. Some Roman harbour walls have stood in seawater for two thousand years.

beats.speaker: q
beats.text: What's the best example?

beats.speaker: a
beats.text: The Pantheon in Rome. Its dome, finished under Emperor Hadrian around AD 126, is still the largest unreinforced concrete dome in the world.
beats.say: The Pantheon in Rome. Its dome, finished under Emperor Hadrian around A D one twenty-six, is still the largest unreinforced concrete dome in the world.

beats.speaker: q
beats.text: How big is it?

beats.speaker: a
beats.text: Forty-three metres across, and exactly as tall as it is wide, so a giant ball would fit inside. And there's no steel in it at all.

beats.speaker: q
beats.text: So what was the secret?

beats.speaker: a
beats.text: Volcanic ash from near Naples, mixed with lime. And in 2023, scientists at MIT showed the Romans used hot quicklime, which left tiny white lumps in the concrete.
beats.say: Volcanic ash from near Naples, mixed with lime. And in twenty twenty-three, scientists at M I T showed the Romans used hot quicklime, which left tiny white lumps in the concrete.

beats.speaker: a
beats.text: When water seeps into a crack, those lumps dissolve and seal it again. In their lab, cracked samples healed themselves within two weeks.

beats.speaker: q
beats.text: So why do modern buildings crack?

beats.speaker: a
beats.text: Most modern concrete hides steel bars inside. When water reaches the steel, it rusts, swells and breaks the concrete apart. Roman concrete had no steel to rust.

beats.speaker: q
beats.text: What about Roman roads?

beats.speaker: a
beats.text: The Romans built more than eighty thousand kilometres of stone-paved roads. The most famous, the Via Appia, was begun in 312 BC, and you can still walk on parts of it.
beats.say: The Romans built more than eighty thousand kilometres of stone-paved roads. The most famous, the Via Appia, was begun in three twelve BC, and you can still walk on parts of it.

beats.speaker: a
beats.text: Each road was built in layers: a deep trench, rubble, gravel, concrete, and finally tightly fitted paving stones.

beats.speaker: q
beats.text: And water?

beats.speaker: a
beats.text: Aqueducts. They carried water into cities using nothing but gravity, sometimes across giant bridges like the Pont du Gard in France.

beats.speaker: q
beats.text: Do any still work?

beats.speaker: a
beats.text: One does. The Aqua Virgo, built by Agrippa in 19 BC, was restored, and its water still feeds the Trevi Fountain in Rome.
beats.say: One does. The Aqua Virgo, built by Agrippa in nineteen BC, was restored, and its water still feeds the Trevi Fountain in Rome.

beats.speaker: a
beats.text: Like the video and follow History Sketches for the next episode: Pompeii.

beats.speaker: q
beats.text: And tell us in the comments: which Roman invention would you bring back?

beats.speaker: a
beats.text: So next time you see a crack in a new building, remember this:
